pages.title: GIT WORKFLOWS CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: Branch, integrate, undo and rescue with confidence
pages.learner: I rebased main and broke everything!

panels.heading: Feature Branch + PR Flow
panels.body:
One branch per change, cut from main.
Push, then open a pull request (PR).
CI (continuous integration) tests it; a teammate reviews.
Merge, then delete the branch.
panels.code:
git switch -c feat/search
git push -u origin feat/search
panels.diagram: Main line of commits; a short cyan branch 'feat/search' with 2 commits; a PR card on top with a green CI check and a reviewer approval stamp; arrow merging back into main and the branch fading out (deleted).

panels.heading: Trunk-Based Development
panels.body:
Everyone merges small changes to main daily.
Branches live hours, not weeks.
Feature flags hide unfinished work.
Main is always releasable.
panels.diagram: Side-by-side timelines: left 'long-lived branches' diverging for weeks with a red conflict explosion at merge; right 'trunk' as one straight line with many tiny branch ticks rejoining within hours and a toggle switch labeled 'flag: off'.

panels.heading: Merge vs Rebase
panels.body:
Merge: joins histories with a merge commit; nothing is rewritten.
Rebase: replays your commits on a new base; new hashes, linear log.
Golden rule: never rebase commits others have already pulled.
panels.code:
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
git push --force-with-lease
panels.diagram: Two mini commit graphs from the same start (main A-B-E, feature C-D). Left 'merge': C-D joined to E by a merge commit M. Right 'rebase': C'-D' re-attached after E in a straight line, original C-D shown as faded ghosts. Golden-rule banner in amber.

panels.heading: Resolve a Merge Conflict
panels.body:
Both branches changed line 12 of config.py.
Git marks it: <<<<<<< HEAD (yours), ======= , >>>>>>> feat/retry (theirs).
Keep the right text, delete all three markers.
Stage the file, then continue.
panels.code:
git status
git add config.py
git merge --continue
panels.diagram: Editor excerpt of config.py: '<<<<<<< HEAD' / 'timeout = 30' / '=======' / 'timeout = 60' / '>>>>>>> feat/retry', with an arrow to the resolved file showing just 'timeout = 60' and a green check.

panels.heading: Stash & Cherry-Pick
panels.body:
Urgent bug mid-feature? Stash edits (-u adds untracked), fix, pop.
Cherry-pick copies one commit to another branch, e.g. a hotfix onto release/2.4, with a new hash.
panels.code:
git stash push -u -m "wip"
git stash pop
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d
panels.diagram: A drawer labeled 'stash' swallowing half-done files; beside it, commit a1b2c3d on main copied as a1b2c3d' onto a 'release/2.4' branch with a copy icon.

panels.heading: Reset vs Revert
panels.body:
reset moves the branch pointer back: rewrites history, keep it local.
revert adds a new commit that undoes an old one: safe when shared.
--soft keeps changes staged; --hard deletes them.
panels.code:
git reset --soft HEAD~1
git revert 9f8e7d6
panels.diagram: Two tracks: 'reset' shows the branch label sliding back from D to C with D greyed out (local only); 'revert' shows A-B-C-D followed by a new commit D' labeled 'undo D' (public, safe).

panels.heading: Reflog Rescue
panels.body:
Reflog records every local move of HEAD.
Lost commits after a bad reset or rebase? Point a branch at the old entry.
Uncommitted changes are never in reflog.
panels.diagram: A rewind tape labeled 'reflog' listing HEAD@{0} reset, HEAD@{1} rebase, HEAD@{2} commit: add search; a rescue rope pulling commit e4f5a6b back onto a new branch 'rescue'.

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Check Yourself
panels.body:
Force-push to main: block it with branch protection.
Prefer --force-with-lease over --force.
Weeks-old branches = painful conflicts.
Quiz: bad commit already on shared main. Reset or revert? (Revert.)
panels.diagram: Warning sign with a shattered 'main' branch and 'git push --force' crossed out in red; a small quiz card with 'reset?' crossed out and 'revert' circled in green.

pages.footer: Branch small, merge often, revert in public, reflog to rescue.
pages.summary: Team Git workflows: feature-branch pull requests versus trunk-based development, when to merge or rebase (and the golden rule), resolving conflicts, stash and cherry-pick, reset versus revert, and recovering lost commits with reflog.

pages.title: DOCKER CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: Package once, run the same everywhere
pages.learner: Why does it only work on my machine?

panels.heading: Containers vs VMs
panels.body:
VM (virtual machine): full guest OS on a hypervisor; GBs, boots in minutes.
Container: isolated process sharing the host kernel; MBs, starts in about a second.
Isolation comes from Linux namespaces and cgroups.
panels.diagram: Two stacks side by side. VM stack: hardware -> host OS -> hypervisor -> three boxes each with its own guest OS + libs + app. Container stack: hardware -> host OS kernel -> container engine -> three slim boxes with libs + app only. Size labels 'GBs' vs 'MBs'.

panels.heading: Image vs Container
panels.body:
Image: read-only template (app + libraries + config).
Container: a running instance of an image plus a thin writable layer.
One image -> many containers, like class -> objects.
panels.diagram: One violet image box labeled 'shop:1.0 (read-only)' with three arrows to three running containers, each with a thin cyan 'writable layer' on top.

panels.heading: Dockerfile Instructions
panels.body:
FROM picks a base image; WORKDIR sets the folder.
COPY adds files; RUN executes at build time.
ENV sets variables; EXPOSE documents a port.
CMD is the default command at run time.
panels.code:
FROM python:3.13-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
panels.diagram: A Dockerfile card with each instruction keyword color-coded and a small icon: FROM (foundation block), WORKDIR (folder), COPY (file arrow), RUN (gear), ENV (key=value tag), EXPOSE (port plug), CMD (play button).

panels.heading: Layers & Build Cache
panels.body:
RUN, COPY and ADD each create a cached layer.
A change rebuilds that layer and all layers after it.
So install dependencies first, copy source last: editing app.py skips the slow pip step.
panels.code:
# continued from panel 3
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
panels.diagram: Stacked layer bricks bottom-up: base image, pip install (green 'CACHED'), COPY . . (amber 'REBUILT' after editing app.py). A red side note shows the wrong order where COPY . . sits below pip install and both rebuild.

panels.heading: Build, Run, Inspect
panels.body:
-t names the image; -d runs it in the background.
-p 8080:8000 maps host port 8080 to container port 8000.
docker ps lists running containers (-a: all).
panels.code:
docker build -t shop:1.0 .
docker run -d -p 8080:8000 --name shop shop:1.0
docker logs -f shop
docker exec -it shop sh
panels.diagram: Pipeline: Dockerfile -> 'docker build' -> image shop:1.0 -> 'docker run' -> container 'shop'. A browser at localhost:8080 connected through a port tunnel to :8000 inside the container; side icons for logs (scroll) and exec (terminal).

panels.heading: Registries & Tags
panels.body:
Registry = image store (Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR).
Full name = registry/repo:tag.
Tags are movable labels; pin a digest (@sha256:...) for an exact image.
panels.code:
docker tag shop:1.0 ghcr.io/acme/shop:1.0
docker push ghcr.io/acme/shop:1.0
docker pull ghcr.io/acme/shop:1.0
panels.diagram: Laptop pushing an image crate up to a cloud warehouse labeled 'registry'; a server pulling it down. The name ghcr.io/acme/shop:1.0 split into labeled parts: registry / repo / tag. A sticky-note tag vs a fingerprint labeled digest.

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Check Yourself
panels.body:
latest is just a default tag, not 'newest'.
Container files vanish on removal: use volumes.
Never bake secrets into layers; add a .dockerignore.
Quiz: you edit app.py. Which steps rebuild? (COPY . . onward.)
panels.diagram: Warning icons: a 'latest' tag with a question mark, a container dissolving with files falling out next to a safe volume drum, a key stuck inside a layer brick crossed out in red.

pages.footer: Build the image once, ship it, run it anywhere.
pages.summary: Docker basics: how containers differ from virtual machines, images versus containers, Dockerfile instructions and layer caching, the build/run/logs/exec workflow, and pushing tagged images to a registry.

pages.title: DOCKER COMPOSE CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: Run a whole multi-container app from one file
pages.learner: Do I start every container by hand?

panels.heading: Why Compose
panels.body:
Real apps need several containers: web, database, cache.
Compose describes them all in compose.yaml.
One command builds, wires, starts and stops the stack.
panels.diagram: Before/after: left, a tangle of separate 'docker run' commands with cables; right, a single compose.yaml scroll feeding three neat containers web, db, cache.

panels.heading: Services, Networks, Volumes
panels.body:
Service: one container's config (image, ports, env).
Network: services share a default network and reach each other by name, e.g. cache:6379.
Volume: named storage that survives container removal.
panels.diagram: Three labeled boxes web, cache, db inside a dashed 'default network' boundary with name-based arrows (web -> cache:6379); a barrel-shaped volume 'cache-data' attached to cache, outside the container.

panels.heading: A compose.yaml Example
panels.body:
web builds from ./Dockerfile; host 8080 -> container 8000.
cache runs Redis; web connects to redis://cache:6379.
Volume cache-data keeps data across restarts.
panels.diagram: The YAML card with arrows: 'web' line -> container built from a Dockerfile icon with port 8080->8000; 'cache' line -> Redis container plugged into a 'cache-data' drum.

panels.heading: Env & Secrets
panels.body:
environment: inline variables.
env_file: loads .env (never commit it).
secrets: mounted as files in /run/secrets/, not env vars.
Declare each secret at top level, e.g. file: ./db_password.txt.
panels.code:
# under services.web:
environment: {LOG_LEVEL: info}
env_file: .env
secrets: [db_password]
panels.diagram: Three inputs flowing into the web container: a tag 'LOG_LEVEL=info', a .env file with a Git icon crossed out, and a locked envelope landing at /run/secrets/db_password.

panels.heading: Multi-Stage Builds
panels.body:
Stage 1 has the compiler and tools; the final stage copies only the binary.
Result: smaller, safer image, e.g. 900 MB -> 15 MB.
End with ENTRYPOINT ["/app"].
panels.code:
FROM golang:1.26 AS build
# copy source, go build -o /app
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /app /app
panels.diagram: Two-stage factory: a big 'build' room full of tools (compiler, source, caches, 900 MB) passes one small box '/app' through a hatch to a tiny final image (15 MB) that ships.

panels.heading: Healthchecks & depends_on
panels.body:
depends_on alone only orders startup; it does not wait for readiness.
Add a healthcheck plus condition: service_healthy.
Now web starts after cache answers PONG.
panels.diagram: Timeline: cache starts -> health light turns from amber 'starting' to green 'healthy' after a PING/PONG bubble -> only then the web container powers on.

panels.heading: Everyday Commands
panels.body:
up -d starts in background; --build rebuilds images.
docker compose exec web sh opens a shell.
down removes containers and network; -v also deletes volumes.
panels.code:
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f web
docker compose down
panels.diagram: Control panel with four big buttons labeled up, ps, logs, down; a red guarded switch labeled 'down -v (deletes data)'.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
localhost inside a container means that container: use service names.
Committing .env with real passwords.
down -v wipes your database.
Compose suits dev and single hosts; clusters need Kubernetes.
panels.diagram: Red warning cards: a web container calling 'localhost' and hitting itself in a loop; a .env file leaking into a Git repo; a database drum being shredded by 'down -v'.

pages.footer: One compose.yaml, one command, the whole stack.
pages.summary: Docker Compose for multi-container apps: services, networks and volumes in compose.yaml, environment variables and secrets, multi-stage builds for small images, healthchecks with depends_on, and the everyday compose commands.

pages.title: KUBERNETES CORE CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: Declare the state you want; the cluster keeps it
pages.learner: Who restarts my containers at 3 a.m.?

panels.heading: Why Orchestration
panels.body:
100 containers on 20 machines: who places, restarts and scales them?
Kubernetes (K8s) automates scheduling, self-healing, scaling and rollouts.
You declare what you want; it makes it happen.
panels.diagram: A frazzled operator juggling container boxes across server racks (left) vs a calm conductor robot labeled 'Kubernetes' arranging the same boxes on nodes (right).

panels.heading: Control Plane
panels.body:
API server: the front door; every kubectl call goes here.
etcd: key-value store holding cluster state.
Scheduler: picks a node for each new Pod.
Controller manager: loops that fix drift.
panels.diagram: A control tower with four labeled rooms: API server (door, kubectl arrow in), etcd (database cylinder), scheduler (placing a Pod onto a node map), controller manager (spinning loop arrows). Only the API server talks to etcd.

panels.heading: Worker Nodes
panels.body:
Node = a machine (VM or bare metal) that runs Pods.
kubelet: agent that starts containers via the runtime (containerd) and reports status.
kube-proxy: network rules that route Service traffic to Pods.
panels.diagram: A node box containing kubelet (robot foreman reporting to the API server), container runtime (engine), kube-proxy (traffic signs), and two Pods with containers inside.

panels.heading: Pod -> ReplicaSet -> Deployment
panels.body:
Pod: smallest unit; 1+ containers sharing an IP and volumes. Disposable.
ReplicaSet: keeps N identical Pods running.
Deployment: manages ReplicaSets for rolling updates and rollback.
You write Deployments, rarely bare Pods.
panels.diagram: Nested boxes: outer 'Deployment web' -> 'ReplicaSet web-7d9f (replicas: 3)' -> three Pods, each holding a container 'shop:1.0'. An older faded ReplicaSet at 0 replicas kept for rollback.

panels.heading: Service Types
panels.body:
Pods come and go with new IPs; a Service gives a stable name and virtual IP.
ClusterIP: internal only (default).
NodePort: a port (30000-32767) on every node.
LoadBalancer: provisions a cloud load balancer.
panels.diagram: Three stacked lanes: ClusterIP (traffic only inside the cluster boundary), NodePort (arrow entering node:30080), LoadBalancer (internet cloud -> load balancer -> nodes). Each Service fans out to Pods labeled app: web.

panels.heading: Reconciliation Loop
panels.body:
Desired state (stored in etcd) vs actual state (what runs).
Controllers watch, compare, act, repeat.
Example: replicas: 3, a node dies, 2 Pods left -> controller creates 1 more.
panels.diagram: Circular loop: observe -> diff (want 3, have 2) -> act (create Pod) -> back to observe. A crashed node with an X; a new Pod appearing on a healthy node.

panels.heading: A Deployment in YAML
panels.body:
Also set apiVersion: apps/v1 and metadata.name: web.
The Pod template is labeled app: web and runs image shop:1.0.
The selector must match those labels.
kubectl apply -f web.yaml -> 3 Pods.
panels.code:
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}
panels.diagram: YAML card with arrows: 'replicas: 3' -> three Pod icons; 'matchLabels app: web' -> a magnifier matching the label tag 'app: web' on each Pod; a template stamp printing Pods from image shop:1.0.

panels.heading: Namespaces & Pitfalls
panels.body:
Namespaces split one cluster into groups (dev, prod, team-a) with separate names and quotas.
Pitfalls: bare Pods are not recreated.
Selector-label mismatch = no Pods managed.
Don't hand-edit what a controller owns.
panels.diagram: One cluster box divided into colored rooms dev / prod / team-a; red warning icons for a lone Pod falling with no ReplicaSet net and mismatched label tags 'app: web' vs 'app: api'.

pages.footer: You declare the desired state; controllers loop until reality matches.
pages.summary: Core Kubernetes: why container orchestration exists, the control plane and worker node components, Pods, ReplicaSets and Deployments, Service types, namespaces, and the desired-state reconciliation loop, with a Deployment YAML example.

pages.title: KUBERNETES IN PRACTICE
pages.subtitle: Configure, expose, scale and debug real workloads
pages.learner: Why is my Pod in CrashLoopBackOff?

panels.heading: kubectl Essentials
panels.body:
get lists resources; describe shows details and events.
logs --previous prints the last crashed run.
apply -f makes the cluster match your files.
panels.code:
kubectl get pods -n shop
kubectl describe pod web-7d9f-x2k
kubectl logs web-7d9f-x2k --previous
kubectl apply -f k8s/
panels.diagram: A terminal window with the four commands, each with a small icon: list, magnifier with event timeline, scroll of logs, and a sync arrow from a folder 'k8s/' to the cluster.

panels.heading: ConfigMaps & Secrets
panels.body:
ConfigMap: non-secret settings, e.g. LOG_LEVEL=info.
Secret: passwords and tokens; only base64-encoded, so enable encryption at rest and RBAC (role-based access control).
Inject as env vars or mounted files.
panels.code:
kubectl create configmap app-cfg --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info
kubectl create secret generic db-cred --from-file=password=./pw.txt
panels.diagram: Two cards feeding a Pod: an open note 'ConfigMap app-cfg: LOG_LEVEL=info' and a padlocked envelope 'Secret db-cred' with a small warning 'base64 is not encryption'; arrows into env vars and a mounted file path.

panels.heading: Ingress
panels.body:
One HTTP(S) entry point; routes by host and path to Services.
shop.example.com/api -> api; / -> web.
Needs an ingress controller; Gateway API is the successor.
panels.diagram: Internet traffic entering one gate labeled 'Ingress shop.example.com'; signposts split '/api' to the api Service and '/' to the web Service, each fanning out to Pods. A small lock for TLS.

panels.heading: Liveness & Readiness Probes
panels.body:
Readiness fails -> Pod gets no traffic, keeps running.
Liveness fails -> kubelet restarts the container.
Startup probe: grace time for slow starts.
panels.code:
readinessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /ready, port: 8000}}
livenessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8000}}
panels.diagram: Two gauges on a Pod: 'readiness' red -> traffic arrow from the Service detached (Pod still running); 'liveness' red -> restart icon on the container. A timer labeled 'startup probe' before them.

panels.heading: Requests & Limits
panels.body:
Request: reserved share; the scheduler uses it to place Pods.
Limit: hard cap. Over memory -> OOMKilled (out of memory); over CPU -> throttled.
250m = 0.25 of a CPU core.
panels.diagram: A node's capacity bar with Pods packed by their requests; one container's memory gauge passing the 512Mi red line -> 'OOMKilled' stamp; a CPU gauge at its limit shown as a throttled, slowed arrow.

panels.heading: HPA Autoscaling
panels.body:
HPA = Horizontal Pod Autoscaler: adds or removes Pods from metrics.
Target 70% CPU, average at 140% -> replicas double, 3 -> 6.
Needs CPU requests and metrics-server.
panels.code: kubectl autoscale deployment web --cpu=70% --min=2 --max=10
panels.diagram: Graph of CPU load rising past a 70% target line; the Pod row grows from 3 to 6. Formula callout: desired = ceil(3 x 140 / 70) = 6, clamped between min 2 and max 10.

panels.heading: Rolling Updates, Rollback, Helm
panels.body:
A new image replaces Pods gradually; traffic keeps flowing.
Bad release? Undo to the previous ReplicaSet.
Helm = package manager for templated YAML charts.
panels.code:
kubectl set image deployment/web web=shop:1.1
kubectl rollout status deployment/web
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web
helm upgrade --install shop ./chart
panels.diagram: Row of Pods changing color one by one from v1.0 (violet) to v1.1 (cyan) while traffic continues; a rewind button 'rollout undo' returning to violet; a Helm chart box stamping out templated YAML.

panels.heading: Pitfall: CrashLoopBackOff
panels.body:
Container keeps exiting; restart delays grow (up to 5 min).
Check logs --previous and describe.
Exit 137 = killed (often OOMKilled); 1 = app error.
Causes: bad config, missing Secret, strict liveness probe.
panels.diagram: Detective robot with a checklist next to a Pod looping start -> crash -> wait 10s, 20s, 40s ... 5m; clues on the board: 'Exit 137 OOMKilled', 'Secret not found', 'liveness failed'.

pages.footer: Probe it, size it, scale it; read events when it breaks.
pages.summary: Running real workloads on Kubernetes: everyday kubectl commands, ConfigMaps and Secrets, Ingress routing, liveness and readiness probes, resource requests and limits, HPA autoscaling, rolling updates and rollback, Helm, and debugging CrashLoopBackOff.
